metaDescription: Five Makita cordless hedge trimmers from 18V LXT to 40V XGT, kit or bare tool, compared on blade length, speed and which battery family you already own.
expertTake: The 40V XGT 24 inch trimmer is the best Makita here if you want three speeds and long runtime, and the brushless XHU09Z is the best choice for owners of 18V LXT batteries. The XHU10SM1 kit is the best first purchase for someone with no Makita packs. Anyone who only trims a few shrubs should buy the 2-in-1 shear instead.
introParagraphs: A maker with two battery families sells overlapping hedge trimmers, and the labels do not make the differences obvious. The smaller-voltage platform is the larger, older system with a wide range of tools, while the higher-voltage line is newer and aimed at heavier work.

For most buyers the first decision is which batteries they already own, since a bare tool is only good value with matching packs. After that, blade length, motor type and speed control separate the models.

products.name: Makita 40V Max XGT 24 in. Brushless Cordless Hedge Trimmer, Bare Tool

specList.label: Claimed runtime
specList.value: Up to 6 h on a 4.0Ah pack

products.description:
The three-speed selector is what separates this trimmer from every other Makita here. Low is 2,000 strokes per minute, medium 3,600 and high 5,000, so you can slow the blades for soft growth to save charge and speed them up for dense tops. The brushless motor is Makita-built and keeps its speed better under load than a brushed design.

The maker claims up to 6 hours of runtime on a 40V XGT 4.0Ah battery, which should be read as a best case at low speed. The tool is sold bare, and XGT packs are not the same family as the 18V LXT range, so an owner of the smaller packs must buy a new battery and charger. At 24 inches the head is long and heavy, so it suits waist to chest height work.

Compared with the XHU09Z 18V LXT trimmer, the XGT is faster and has more runtime headroom, but it ties you to a battery family that has fewer tools than LXT. Wipe the blades after each use, oil them and do not leave the pack on the charger for weeks. It is the pick for someone building a 40V Makita line. A practical habit is to run low speed for the first pass over a freshly grown top and switch to high only where the blade starts to bog down. That habit stretches a 4.0Ah pack much further than leaving the dial on maximum all session.
products.bestFor: Owners of 40V XGT batteries who hedge long runs.
pros: Three speed settings from 2,000 to 5,000 SPM
Brushless motor holds speed under load
Claimed runtime of up to 6 hours
24 inch blade for wide passes
cons: XGT packs do not fit 18V LXT tools
Sold bare with no battery or charger

products.name: Makita XHU09Z 18V LXT Brushless Cordless 24 in. Hedge Trimmer, Tool Only
products.description:
Makita lists this as a brushless 24 inch trimmer on the 18V LXT platform, and for owners of that battery family it is the most efficient way to add a hedge tool. A brushless motor wastes less energy as heat and has no carbon brushes to wear out, which matters on a tool that works in short, hard bursts.

The LXT platform is the real value. These batteries run a wide range of Makita tools, including drills, blowers and saws, so a household with a few of them can add a hedge trimmer for the price of the bare tool. A first-time buyer pays for the pack and charger on top.

At 24 inches the blade is the same length as the XGT and the XHU10 models, so the choice among them is about motor type and platform, not reach. Check the listing for cut capacity before ordering, since it is not stated in the data we saw. Wipe the blades after use and keep the pack indoors in winter. Because LXT is the larger family, spare packs and chargers are easy to find at most tool dealers, which means a dead battery in year four is a small problem, not a stranded tool. A rapid charger is worth buying if you plan to work through a long hedge with two packs.
products.bestFor: 18V LXT owners who want a brushless hedge trimmer.
pros: Brushless motor runs cooler and lasts longer
Runs on the common 18V LXT batteries
24 inch blade for fast passes
No gas, oil mixing or pull starts
cons: Sold bare with no battery or charger
Capacity is not stated in the listing

products.name: Makita XHU10SM1 18V LXT 24 in. Cordless Hedge Trimmer Kit, 4.0Ah
products.description:
This is the Makita for someone who owns no Makita batteries. The kit includes a 4.0Ah 18V LXT battery and a charger with the 24 inch hedge trimmer, so you can cut as soon as it arrives. A 4.0Ah pack is a sensible size for a hedge tool, bigger than the 2.0Ah packs in most budget kits.

It is the same tool as the XHU10Z bare unit, which is sold on its own for people with batteries. If you do not own LXT packs, buying the kit is cheaper than buying the bare tool and a pack separately. The listing highlights the benefits of cordless in general: no gas, no oil mixing, no pull starts and low noise.

The 4.0Ah pack will handle a modest garden in one charge, but a long boundary hedge will want a second pack. Keep the battery indoors, oil the blades after use and clear clippings from the vents. Because the platform is LXT, any later Makita purchases can share the same battery. If you later add the brushless XHU09Z or a Makita blower, you will already own the pack and charger, so the second purchase costs much less than the first. It is a low-risk way to enter a large platform, which is why we rank it as the best first purchase.

products.name: Makita XHU10Z 18V LXT Cordless 24 in. Hedge Trimmer, Tool Only

specList.label: Noise
specList.value: Low, no gas or pull start

products.description:
The XHU10Z is the bare version of the kit above, and the right choice if you already own LXT packs. It carries the same 24 inch blade, and the listing highlights the same benefits: no gas, no oil mixing and low noise.

Next to the brushless XHU09Z, it is the simpler, older design, and the listing does not describe the motor as brushless. That means it will run a little warmer and with less efficiency than the XHU09Z, which matters if you cut every week and less if you trim a couple of times a year. In that situation the price difference may be reason enough to choose it.

There is nothing to maintain beyond blade care and battery storage. Oil the blades after each use, keep the guard straight and avoid forcing the tool through stems thicker than the gap. If you own LXT packs and trim lightly, this is the cheapest way into a 24 inch Makita. Treat the listing's claims about low noise and reduced maintenance as the general benefits of any battery tool, and judge it on blade, battery and price. If it ever feels underpowered, check the blade for resin before suspecting the motor, because dirty teeth cause most of the stalling that owners complain about.
products.bestFor: Light users who already have LXT batteries.
pros: 24 inch blade with a quiet cordless motor
Runs on existing 18V LXT packs
No fuel or oil mixing
Simpler than the brushless model

products.name: Makita XMU04ZX 18V LXT Cordless Grass Shear with Hedge Trimmer Blade, Tool Only

specList.label: Claimed runtime
specList.value: Up to 3 h on a 5.0Ah pack

products.description:
This is a shear that accepts a hedge trimmer blade, not a full-size hedge trimmer. A quick blade change switches between a grass shear and a hedge blade, and the Makita-built motor delivers up to 2,500 strokes per minute.

It is the choice for detail: shaping box, trimming lavender or edging a border. The maker claims up to 3 hours of runtime on a 5.0Ah LXT battery, which reflects how little power a small blade draws. Because the blade is small, it is lighter and easier on the wrists than the 24 inch trimmers.

It will not replace a hedge trimmer on a boundary hedge, and it is not meant to. Use the full-length XHU models for that and keep this one for precision. Clean the blades after each use and store the battery away from frost. Switching blades is a tool-free job, but always remove the battery first, since a blade that moves while you swap it is a real injury risk. Owners often keep this shear mounted with the grass blade and swap to the hedge blade only when shaping.
products.bestFor: Shaping shrubs and edging borders with minimal strain.
pros: Quick blade change between shear and hedge blade
Up to 2,500 SPM motor
Light and easy on the wrists
Claimed runtime of up to 3 hours
cons: Blade is too small for long hedges

buyingCriteria.explanation: Makita sells hedge trimmers on 18V LXT and 40V XGT. LXT batteries run a large range of tools, while XGT is newer and aimed at heavier work. Choose the platform that matches your existing batteries, since the packs are not interchangeable.

The XHU09Z and the 40V XGT are brushless, while the XHU10Z is not described that way. A brushless motor runs cooler and wastes less energy. It matters most if you cut often or work through thick growth.
Only the 40V XGT offers three speeds at 2,000, 3,600 and 5,000 SPM. A slower setting saves battery on soft growth. The 2-in-1 shear tops out at 2,500 SPM, which suits small work.

The XHU10SM1 includes a 4.0Ah battery and charger, while the XHU10Z, XHU09Z, XMU04ZX and the XGT are bare tools. A bare tool saves money only if you own packs. Add the cost of a battery and charger to any bare tool before you compare. Many buyers discover the omission at the checkout, so read the listing title for the words tool only before you add anything to the basket.

Four of the five picks use a 24 inch blade, which covers a top fast but weighs more at arm's length. The XMU04ZX is a small-blade shear. Pick the 24 inch models for waist to chest height work and the shear for detail.

Makita claims up to 6 hours on a 4.0Ah XGT pack and up to 3 hours on a 5.0Ah LXT pack for the shear. These are best-case figures at low load. Dense hedge shortens them a lot. Cold mornings and old packs shorten them further, so plan your first season's work around half of any quoted figure and adjust upward only if you find it holds. A second battery is the easiest cure for any runtime worry.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared LXT and XGT options and whether a battery is included. The XHU10SM1 scored high as a complete kit. The bare tools scored lower for newcomers.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared brushless motors and speed range. The XGT with three speeds led, followed by the brushless XHU09Z.

howWeEvaluated.title: Blade length and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 24 inch blades with the small shear. Longer blades covered more but weighed more at arm's length.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the maker's runtime figures against battery size. The 6 hour claim on a 4.0Ah XGT pack scored well but was treated as a best case.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered blade care, battery storage and platform breadth. LXT scored well for the number of tools it runs. We also looked at how simple each tool is to service, since a trimmer with a single drive and no fuel system leaves little to go wrong. A tool that arrives with a battery counted for more than one that needs a separate purchase.

cards.label: Brushless
cards.text: The XHU09Z and XGT run cooler, last longer and hold speed under load. They suit frequent use and thick growth.

cards.label: Brushed
cards.text: The XHU10Z and the 2-in-1 shear are simpler and cheaper. They suit light, occasional work.

howToChoose.note: Choose brushless if you hedge weekly and brushed if you hedge a few times a year.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a long blade, a brushless motor and enough battery capacity to finish a long run. Speed control that lets you save charge on soft growth is a bonus.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Makita 40V XGT 24 in. offers three speeds and a claimed 6 hours on a 4.0Ah pack. The XHU09Z is the LXT alternative if you own those packs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you hedge often. The brushless XHU09Z or the three-speed XGT are the models that justify a higher cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you own LXT batteries and trim lightly. The XHU10Z bare tool or the XMU04ZX shear are cheaper.

maintenance.why: Sap hardens on the teeth and cuts capacity. Oil protects the steel.
Clippings trap heat around the motor. Brush them out with the battery removed.
Cold lowers capacity. Keep at half charge.
A bent guard causes stalling. Replace if it will not straighten. Check it after any contact with wire fences or trellis, which is the usual way a guard gets bent without you noticing.
Loose bolts let the blades gap and tear stems. Use the maker's torque guidance and avoid over-tightening, which makes the blades bind and draw more current from the battery.

faq.q: Should I buy LXT or XGT?
faq.a: Buy whichever matches the batteries you own. If you own none, the XHU10SM1 kit is the simplest start, and the XGT trimmer is the choice if you plan a larger 40V line. Think about the tools you are likely to add in the next five years, because a battery family is a long commitment. Makita keeps both platforms supported, so neither choice is a dead end.

faq.q: Is the XGT trimmer worth the extra?
faq.a: If you hedge long runs, yes. Its three speeds and brushless motor give more control and runtime than the 18V models.

faq.q: What is the difference between the XHU10Z and XHU10SM1?
faq.a: They are the same 24 inch tool. The Z is bare, and the SM1 includes a 4.0Ah battery and charger.

faq.q: Can the shear replace a hedge trimmer?
faq.a: No. The XMU04ZX is a small-blade shear for detail and edging, not for a boundary hedge.

faq.q: How long will a pack last?
faq.a: Makita claims up to 6 hours on a 4.0Ah XGT pack and up to 3 hours for the shear on a 5.0Ah pack. These are best-case figures, and dense growth will cut them.

Only soft stems up to the blade gap, which the listings do not state for all models. Use loppers for anything thicker than a finger. Overloading a hedge blade with woody stems dulls the teeth quickly and can strain the gear stage, so cut thick growth by hand and let the trimmer do the finishing work. A cut that leaves frayed, torn ends is a sign the blades are dull or dirty.
